item.title: Microsoft security advisory – November 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1142) – Update 1
Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments.

“The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises.

The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings.

A security company that wants to run models

Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.”

“Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from.

Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building.

“I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025.

“A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result.

GPUs and data centers

To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years.

Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from.

“A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said.

Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.

One vendor, more of the stack

The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk, which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls.

“Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.”

CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.

item.title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Europol-coordinated global crackdown
item.description: Europol, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, have successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offences. The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide.

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: Investment scams with potential victims in at least 50 countries: over 100 servers seized
item.description: Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets. Seven suspects...

item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
item.description:
PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

  • The threat actor gets in through the web application.
  • Reads the configuration file;
  • Dumps the customer database;
  • Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

  • Is session upload progress on?
  • Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?
  • Does php-cgi face the internet?
  • Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

item.title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
item.description:
The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.

“Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush, Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post. “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.”

Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do

WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025.

WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository, and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take.

The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address.

This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained.

Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request.

The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors. Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over. 

But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do.

Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.”

Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge.

They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets.

There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work.

Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’

Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability, safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com, github.com, or raw.githubusercontent.com.

Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.”

Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs.

“The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.”

He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.”

Scripts are a soft spot

The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.”

This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets.

And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source.

“The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said.

Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go?

Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said.

Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”

item.title: A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
item.description:
When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE).

With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT.

Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK x86-64 Base64 decoder that scores 9.2 in severity (Critical) under CVSS 4.0, Calif said. Oracle assigned it a lower rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1.

Calif explained in its post describing the issue that Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. “It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” it wrote. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution.”

It said that the corruption can be triggered by a string of just 64 “A” characters followed by a single equals sign (=); in older OpenJDK 17 versions, 128 “A” characters are required before the equals sign.

“Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the internet,” Calif said. “But one of Java’s biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers’ behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.”

Assessing the bug’s potential for exploit is complicated because triggering it requires a hardware accelerated decoding function that’s used on some x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. And fixing it requires patches from a lengthy list of vendors; just installing Tuesday’s patch from Oracle, which owns Java, is not going to do the trick.

Potential damage ‘extreme’

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, said the potential damage from an unpatched instance of exposed Java is extreme.

“The researchers were able to read Java heap memory before they achieved code execution, so an attacker may be able to steal tokens, credentials, or keys from those systems. That access can remain useful even after the vulnerable server has been patched,” Kenney said. “Any unexplained crashes on an exposed system should lead to a review of what secrets were in memory and whether they need to be rotated.”

But not every instance is vulnerable to this flaw. 

“The same Java application and version can be vulnerable on a newer x86 server and unaffected on older hardware because the faulty decoder only runs when AVX-512 is available,” he noted. “That makes a normal software inventory less useful than it usually is. CISOs need to know the Java distribution and version, the processor underneath it, and whether untrusted Base64 reaches the decoder. Installing a newer processor can expose an application that was safe on the server it replaced, without changing the application at all.”

A further complication is that enterprises will also be running Java from a massive array of specialized vendors.

“Oracle released a fix for its Java builds, but enterprises also run Java from Amazon, Eclipse, Microsoft, Red Hat, and Azul, along with runtimes buried inside commercial products and containers,” Kenney pointed out. “CISOs should start with identity systems and software-delivery infrastructure, identify the runtime each one is actually using, apply the appropriate vendor fix, and restart or rebuild the workload.”

He also said that outbound connections need to be evaluated. “Researchers demonstrated that a Java program could be compromised by connecting to a malicious TLS server, even when it had no service exposed to the internet.”

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, agreed, pointing out, “the client-side exploit puts any Java process that connects to a malicious TLS server at risk: integrations, connectors, crawlers and batch jobs. Patch scopes built around internet-facing listeners will miss them.”

Lack of visibility a big problem

Mahapatra also stressed that many Java implementations can be hard to locate. 

“Your SBOM [software bill of materials] can’t see the real exposure. Whether a service is vulnerable depends on the silicon underneath as much as the JDK version,” he said. “The same container image is exploitable on an Ice Lake or Zen 4 node and safe on ARM or older hardware, and autoscaling can move it between the two. For once, the organizations that refreshed their hardware are the exposed ones.”

But it is the lack of visibility that concerns practitioners the most. 

The Java hole “exposes a blind spot in how enterprises identify, prioritize and validate vulnerabilities,” said Raj Annaladasu, staff customer success engineer at Palo Alto Networks. “Enterprise teams invest heavily in application code review, dependency scanning, and secure coding practices. Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerabilities can originate below the application layer, inside the managed runtime itself.”

“This is an important distinction: Java’s memory-safety abstractions do not protect an application from memory corruption originating inside a vulnerable native runtime implementation,” he said. “Applications may be using a standard Java API correctly while the underlying runtime implementation is vulnerable. This shifts the security boundary beyond application code and third-party dependencies to include the runtime, its implementation, and the hardware capabilities that influence execution.”

This means, he said, that exploitability depends on multiple conditions coming together: an affected Java runtime, the relevant CPU instruction capabilities, the vulnerable execution path being enabled, and attacker-controlled input reaching the decoder.

But, he pointed out, “one of the bigger challenges is discovering where Java is actually running. Runtime installations are often bundled inside third-party products, container images, appliances, custom runtime distributions, and application-specific directories. They may not appear as distinct entries in conventional software inventories. A clean application dependency scan or CMDB does not establish that the environment is free of vulnerable Java runtimes.”

Java hides everywhere

Given that there are going to be so many Java vendors, and so many hidden apps, at issue, the risk of a CISO missing a few is massive, noted Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research.

“Java4Shell is a big deal because a single missed server with Java is all an attacker needs, allowing someone who never logs in to read its memory, including personal data, private keys, and tokens,” he said. “From there, the attacker can run code on the server. If that server is an identity system like Keycloak or PingFederate, the attacker now owns you.”

And, he said, it’s highly unlikely that enterprise CISOs will catch all or most Java instances.

“Will a CISO miss one? The odds say yes. Java hides everywhere. Each Java instance needs its own fix,” Dickson said. 

Its popularity is Java’s greatest weakness

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, said Java’s popularity is its biggest weakness.

“Java runs the back office of corporate America: logins, code pipelines, ticketing, internal wikis,” he said. “Java4Shell lets an attacker who hasn’t even logged in take over some of the most sensitive of those systems by sending a short string of text. If your company runs Java on modern servers, and almost every large company does, you’re exposed until you patch.”

He enumerated some examples: “Keycloak and PingFederate control who gets into your company. Jenkins and Artifactory build and store the software you ship. Jira and Confluence hold your roadmaps, incident notes and plenty of passwords people shouldn’t have pasted there,” he said. “Take over those and you aren’t breaking into one room. You’ve stolen the master key, the blueprints and the security guard’s notebook in one move.”

He added, “Java programs that simply connect out to the wrong server can be compromised too. That last one means firewalls and perimeter controls don’t fully protect you.”

However, he pointed out, “there’s one small mercy: the bug only fires on certain newer Intel and AMD chips. The catch is that those chips fill modern data centers and cloud fleets.”

item.title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
item.description:
Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching.

Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5.

Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions.

The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123891), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123892), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123893), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-123894), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them.

Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.”

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

item.title: F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
item.description:
F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic.

All five of the patches are stack-based buffer overflows that could let an unauthenticated threat actor terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

F5 described them as follows:

  • CVE-2026-121805: When an iRule that processes client traffic using the PEM:subscriber command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-120292: When an HTTP profile and an iRule using the MR:message route command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-120285: When an HTTP profile and an iRule containing the PSC:ip_address command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-116953: When an iRule that processes client traffic using the GENERICMESSAGE:route command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-123637: When BIG-IP APM is provisioned and a per-request policy that includes the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE).

The company said there are no mitigations for the flaws and advised customers to install the hotfixes on vulnerable devices, and to upgrade vulnerable versions without a listed fix to a patched version.

In the same batch of out of band patches, F5 also addressed CVE-2026-126822, a high severity integer underflow vulnerability in BIG-IP APM SAML that could also crash TMM and lead to denial of service.

This is the second critical issue in two months for APM; September’s zero-day bug was already being exploited when it was patched. F5 did not indicate that any of the current batch is as yet being exploited but given the growing trend of attacks on edge devices by criminals and nation-state threat actors, admins should update systems as soon as possible.

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

item.title: AL26-029 - Critical vulnerability impacting Oracle Java - CVE-2026-114938
SAP security advisory – November 2025 monthly rollup (AV25-738) – Update 1
